day.d: 30 min: open your own copy of the week's book and hand-copy two pages, longhand. Not typing. You are training the hand and the ear, not the eye. 30 min: rhythm transcription - take a sentence-length pattern and write your own paragraph that matches it exactly.
day.why: Copying by hand is the only exercise that installs cadence below the level of choice. Rhythm transcription gives you the same benefit using your own sentences.

day.d: 20 min flashcards on the Lexicon page until the due queue is empty. 25 min: take the five hardest words from today's session and write three sentences with each - one about work, one about a person, one about your practice. Fifteen sentences.
day.why: A word you have only recognised is not yours. A word you have written three times in your own life is.

day.d: Run the week's assigned drill from the Drills page, start to finish, and apply its success test honestly. If you fail the test, run it again rather than moving on.
day.why: Each drill isolates one mechanic. Isolation is the whole point - you cannot fix six things at once.

day.d: Outside if possible. Do not read anything. Do not listen to a podcast.
day.why: Consolidation happens off-task. This block is not optional and it is not a reward.

day.d: Write on the week's real deliverable - the piece you will publish or send. Draft only. No editing while drafting. Use a Workbench prompt if you are stuck for a subject.
day.why: Drills without shipping produce a technician who has never faced a reader. This is the block that makes the rest real.

day.d: Paste yesterday's draft into the Workbench. Hit every band. Clear every flag. Then do one pass reading only for the mechanic you drilled this week.
day.why: Revising against a number removes the argument. You either hit 68% monosyllables or you did not.

day.d: Read 10 pages of the week's book aloud, at speaking pace. Mark in the margin every time you spot the week's mechanic. Count them at the end.
day.why: Reading aloud catches rhythm your eye skips. Marking the mechanic turns passive admiration into pattern recognition.

day.d: Write 200 words on what you noticed today. What did he do that you would not have thought to do? What did you fail at? Name one thing to carry into tomorrow.
day.why: He calls it his own practice: the day is not finished until it has been looked at.

phases.goal: Strip out everything he dropped. This phase is subtraction only. You will feel like your writing is getting worse before the numbers turn.

w.focus: Semicolons, front-loaded participles, the meaning paragraph, and hedge stacks.
tasks: Purge every semicolon from everything you have ever written
Grep your drafts for a sentence opening with an -ing word plus a comma. Un-invert all of them
Find every paragraph that explains what the previous scene meant. Keep one sentence, delete the rest
w.ship: One 800-word essay with zero semicolons and zero fronted participles

w.focus: Not shorter sentences. Wider range. Learn to write the 30-word sentence and the 4-word sentence, next to each other.
tasks: Twenty verdict beats a day
Push monosyllables past 65% on every draft
Match ten rhythm patterns exactly
w.ship: One 1,000-word piece scoring 70+ in the Workbench

w.focus: The -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity layer. Replace it with the named thing rather than a simpler word.
tasks: Every abstract noun in a draft gets swapped for a named object
Learn all 40 Tier C words and use each once
Seven numerals per 1,000 words
w.ship: A 600-word piece where deleting every adjective loses almost nothing

w.focus: Adjectives are for objects. Numbers are for feelings.
tasks: Zero intensifiers for the whole week, in writing and in speech
Rate yourself numerically instead of describing how something felt
Close three pieces on a clock time
w.ship: A 700-word account of something intense, with zero emotional adjectives

phases.goal: Install the templates. This phase is addition. By the end you should be reaching for these without deciding to.

w.focus: His central rhythmic unit. Long sentence does the world, short sentence does the meaning.
tasks: Twenty beats a day, every day
End-load 20 sentences so the payload lands last
Audit your peaks - they must be plainer than your exposition

w.focus: Handling any unfamiliar term without slowing down. His fastest-growing habit.
tasks: Fifty glosses in thirty minutes, twice this week
Every jargon term in your client work gets an inline gloss
Fifteen cold openings
w.ship: A landing page that explains a technical product with zero parenthetical definitions

w.focus: The image is not the explanation. The restatement in the image's noun is.
tasks: Twelve analogies, every vehicle humbler than its subject
Fifteen re-claim beats
No analogy runs past two sentences
w.ship: An 800-word explainer built on exactly three analogies

w.focus: Where most writers lose the reader, and where he never does.
tasks: Eight openings and eight closings, shuffled and sorted by a friend
Five different closes for one piece
Eight one-breath question cascades
w.ship: Five short pieces, each with a different closing type

phases.goal: The hard part. Stance, authority, restraint, humour. This is what cannot be faked and what took him ten years.

w.focus: Diagnose in we. Prescribe in you. Rank in the third person. The largest single change in fifteen years of his blog.
tasks: Rewrite three old pieces under the we/you rule
Ten echo pivots
Tag every transition in a 2,000-word draft
w.ship: An 1,100-word personal essay with exactly one we-to-you crossover

w.focus: Cost, claim, limit. Concede rather than rebut. Refuse rather than pad.
tasks: Ten cost-claim-limit sequences
Eight conceded objections with zero rebuttals
Twelve refusals
w.ship: A 1,000-word piece making your strongest claim, with one cost sentence and one scope limit

w.focus: Language magnitude must not track event magnitude. And the joke is always on you.
tasks: Five peaks, each followed by something that costs you
Ten two-hander jokes, butt is always the expert
Ten moments of grandeur with zero grandeur words
w.ship: A 1,400-word piece about your worst year, funny in at least three places

w.focus: Everything at once, at length, for a real reader.
tasks: Triage every scene: reported or quoted
Exile every procedure to the end
Rewrite the last line of every section as something unresolved
w.ship: Publish three pieces. Then re-audit week 1's essay and see what you now see.
